UK Economy Faces Growth Squeeze and Higher Inflation From Middle East Conflict, OBR Warns

29 Oct 2026, 05:20 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Business Desk · Source: www.bbc.co.uk

Image: www.bbc.co.uk — Creative Commons

Key takeawaysThe UK economy is experiencing the direct impact of the US-Iran war, with soaring global energy prices threatening short-term growth, pushing up inflation, and putting pressure on living standards, according to official forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibilit

The UK economy is experiencing the direct impact of the US-Iran war, with soaring global energy prices threatening short-term growth, pushing up inflation, and putting pressure on living standards, according to official forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

While the UK has no direct military involvement in the conflict, the fallout is reshaping domestic economic projections. Chancellor John Healey warned that the nation faces "real challenges ahead" driven by global economic instability, noting that the government must carefully steer through these conditions while announcing measures aimed at providing temporary relief for households.

Impact on Growth and Inflation

In its latest assessment, the OBR sharply downgraded its economic growth forecast for next year from 1.6% to 1%, though growth is projected to rebound in subsequent years. Economic growth typically drives business investment, job creation, and wage increases, while higher corporate profits can boost public service funding. However, the current slowdown is accompanied by accelerating price pressures.

The OBR projects that inflation will peak at 3.8% in 2027 as higher energy costs filter through supply chains. Global oil price increases have already affected motorists, with average petrol prices hovering near £1.73 per litre and diesel close to £1.99. Because fuel costs impact transport and logistics, elevated energy expenses are expected to cascade into everyday goods, including food.

Living standards are forecast to experience a dip next year as household spending power is constrained by bills. Lower-income households are expected to bear a disproportionate burden, as energy expenses account for a larger share of their monthly budgets. OBR member David Miles described the broader trajectory as a "grim picture," pointing out that individual living standards have seen virtually no growth since the period prior to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Interest Rates and Government Borrowing

In response to persistent inflation, the Bank of England is widely anticipated to raise interest rates. Rates currently stand at 3.75%, but OBR projections suggest they could climb as high as 4.5% in the coming years, reversing earlier expectations of interest rate cuts. While higher rates increase borrowing costs for mortgages and loans, they can offer improved returns for savers.

The combination of higher inflation and elevated interest rates also increases government debt servicing costs. Consequently, overall government borrowing is predicted to increase each year beyond previous OBR estimates, driven in part by higher inflation-linked spending on welfare and pensions.

Practical Implications and What Remains Uncertain

Confirmed Facts and Figures

  • Growth Downgrade: The OBR lowered its UK growth forecast for next year to 1%.
  • Inflation Peak: Inflation is projected to peak at 3.8% in 2027 before gradually easing toward the Bank of England's 2% target late in the decade.
  • Interest Rates: Forecasts indicate rates could rise as high as 4.5%.
  • Fuel Prices: Average pump prices stand near £1.73 per litre for petrol and £1.99 for diesel.

Unknowns and Variables

  • Geopolitical Shifts: The trajectory of the Middle East conflict remains the primary source of volatility. The OBR acknowledged significant uncertainty in its forecasts, noting that future developments in the region could alter inflation and energy price expectations.
